title: Grade 4 AGRICULTURE — 2.3 Uses of Domestic Animals

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Cattle, sheep, goats and poultry are kept by families and communities. In this sub-strand you will name these domestic animals, match each one to its uses, and explain how they contribute to food through milk, meat, eggs and manure.

## Strand 2.0: Food Production Processes
Sub-strand 2.3: Uses of Domestic Animals
Suggested lessons: 8

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify types of domestic animals in the community
b) relate various domestic animals to their uses
c) appreciate the importance of domestic animals for food production

## Key inquiry questions
1. How do domestic animals contribute to food production?

## Core competencies
• Self-efficacy: self-confidence as learners make presentations on uses of domestic animals.

## Values
• Respect: open mindedness as learners listen and accommodate others opinions during presentations on importance of domestic animals.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Animal welfare as the learners appreciate importance of domestic animals to humans.

## Links to other learning areas
• Learners relate animals reared in their community to knowledge learnt in Social Studies on social economic activities.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Agriculture Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 2.0 Food Production Processes, Sub-strand 2.3 Uses of Domestic Animals

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Domestic animals in the community

LESSON 1: DOMESTIC ANIMALS IN THE COMMUNITY
===========================================

## What you will learn
• Explain the difference between domestic and wild animals.
• Name the domestic animals kept in the community.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify types of domestic animals in the community

## Introduction
A hen that comes when grain is scattered, and a goat that is brought home in the evening, live with people. They are not wild visitors. They are domestic animals.

## Notes
A domestic animal is an animal that people keep and look after. People provide food, water and shelter, and they decide how the animal is used. A wild animal finds its own food and is not owned.

### The animals in this sub-strand
- Cattle include cows, bulls, heifers and oxen. A young cow is a calf.
- Sheep are covered with wool or hair. A young sheep is a lamb.
- Goats are often more agile than sheep and may browse on shrubs. A young goat is a kid.
- Poultry are birds kept by people. Chickens are the most common. Ducks, turkeys and guinea fowl are also poultry. A female chicken is a hen, a male is a cock, and a young one is a chick.

### What you may see in your community
Not every home keeps all four. Some keep only chickens. Some keep goats because they cope where grazing is short. Some keep cattle for milk. Your list should come from animals people in your community really keep, plus the four groups named here so you can talk about them in class.

### Animals that are not this list
Dogs and cats are domestic, but they are not kept mainly for food production. Donkeys may carry loads. Fish are farmed in some places but are not poultry or livestock of the four groups above. For this sub-strand, concentrate on cattle, sheep, goats and poultry.

Look at how the animal is housed or herded. A cow in a boma, a goat on a tether, and hens in a coop are signs that people are responsible for them. That care is the start of animal welfare.

## Key words
• domestic animal — an animal that people keep and care for
• poultry — birds kept by people, such as chickens, ducks and turkeys
• boma — an enclosure where livestock are kept

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner lists a hare, a goat, a monkey and a hen. Which ones are domestic animals?

Working:
1. Goats and hens are kept and cared for by people.
2. Hares and monkeys are wild.

Answer: The goat and the hen.

## Activity: Animals our families keep
You will need: Exercise book, Pictures of cattle, sheep, goats and poultry
1. Name each picture and say whether it is cattle, sheep, goat or poultry.
2. Each learner says which of these animals are kept at home or by a neighbour. Do not invent animals.
3. Make a class tally.
4. Write one sentence that defines a domestic animal and lists the four groups.

## Practice
1. What is a domestic animal?
2. Name four types of domestic animals studied in this sub-strand.
3. Give two examples of poultry.

## Summary
• Domestic animals are kept and cared for by people.
• The four groups here are cattle, sheep, goats and poultry.
• List the animals that are really kept in your community.

### Answers to practice
1. An animal that people keep and look after.
2. Cattle, sheep, goats and poultry.
3. Any two: chickens, ducks, turkeys, guinea fowl.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: Uses of cattle

LESSON 2: USES OF CATTLE
========================

## What you will learn
• Match cattle to the products and work they provide.
• Distinguish a dairy animal from an ox used for work.

Curriculum outcomes: b) relate various domestic animals to their uses

## Introduction
A cow can fill a bucket with milk in the morning. An ox can pull a plough through a seedbed. Both are cattle, but the use the farmer has in mind is not the same.

## Notes
Cattle are kept for several uses. One animal is not always kept for all of them at once.

### Milk
Dairy cattle are kept mainly for milk. Milk is food. It can be drunk fresh after it is handled cleanly, or made into fermented milk and other products. A cow must have had a calf before she gives milk. Clean hands, a clean udder and a clean container keep the milk fit to drink.

### Meat
Cattle kept for meat are beef cattle. The meat is called beef. It is a body-building food because it supplies protein. Hides, the skins of cattle, are used to make leather.

### Work
Oxen are castrated male cattle trained to pull ploughs and carts. They help a farmer prepare land for crops. This is a use of cattle in food production even though the ox itself is not eaten while it is working.

### Manure
Cattle droppings, mixed with bedding and left to rot, become manure. Spread on a garden, manure feeds the soil for maize, vegetables and fruit. This links livestock to crops.

### Matching carefully
A thin cow kept for milk still needs enough feed and water or the milk will be little. A calf is not put to the plough. When you match cattle to uses, say milk, meat, hides, draught power and manure, and say which animal in the herd fits which use.

## Key words
• dairy cattle — cattle kept mainly for milk
• beef — meat from cattle
• draught power — the pulling work done by animals such as oxen

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A family keeps two oxen for ploughing and one cow that is milked each day. Match each animal to its main use.

Working:
1. Oxen are trained to pull ploughs and carts.
2. A cow that is milked is kept for milk.

Answer: The oxen are used for draught power. The cow is used for milk.

## Activity: Cattle use chart
You will need: Manila paper, Pictures or drawings of a cow, an ox, milk, meat, a hide and manure
1. Draw or pin a cow and an ox on the chart.
2. Draw lines to their uses: milk, meat, hides, ploughing and manure.
3. Discuss which uses feed people directly and which help crops grow.
4. Present the chart in one minute.

## Practice
1. Name three uses of cattle.
2. What are oxen mainly used for?
3. How does cattle manure help food production?

## Summary
• Cattle give milk, meat, hides and manure.
• Oxen provide draught power for ploughing and carts.
• Manure links cattle keeping to crop growing.

### Answers to practice
1. Any three: milk, meat, hides, pulling ploughs or carts, manure.
2. Pulling ploughs and carts.
3. It feeds the soil so crops grow better.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Uses of sheep and goats

LESSON 3: USES OF SHEEP AND GOATS
=================================

## What you will learn
• State the uses of sheep and of goats.
• Explain one way goats fit places with shrubs and little grass.

Curriculum outcomes: b) relate various domestic animals to their uses

## Introduction
Sheep and goats are smaller than cattle, so a family with a small piece of land can keep them. Their uses overlap, but they are not the same animal.

## Notes
### Sheep
Sheep are kept mainly for meat, called mutton. Their skins are used for leather. Droppings are used as manure. Some sheep grow wool, which is spun into yarn and used for clothing. Many sheep kept in Kenya are kept first for meat rather than for a heavy wool clip, so do not assume every sheep is a wool sheep. Look at the animals in your own community.

Sheep prefer to graze short grass. They are usually herded in a group called a flock.

### Goats
Goats are kept for meat, and many are also kept for milk. Goat milk is a food, just as cow milk is. Skins are used for leather. Droppings are strong manure and should be composted before they are put on young plants.

Goats browse. They eat leaves and shrubs as well as grass. Because of this they can be kept where the pasture is bushy. They are agile and will eat crops if they are not tethered or housed. A goat in the vegetable garden is not 'using' the goat well. It is a failure of care.

### Comparing them
Both give meat, skins and manure. Goats are the ones more often milked on small farms. Sheep are the ones that may give wool. Neither replaces cattle when a farmer needs a heavy ox for ploughing.

When you match animals to uses, use a table with two columns so sheep and goats are not muddled into one animal.

## Key words
• mutton — meat from sheep
• browse — to eat leaves and twigs of shrubs
• flock — a group of sheep or goats kept together

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A household in a bushy area wants milk and meat from a small animal that can eat shrubs. Should they choose a sheep or a goat? Give one reason.

Working:
1. Goats browse on shrubs and many are kept for milk as well as meat.
2. Sheep mainly graze grass and are kept mainly for meat.

Answer: A goat, because it browses shrubs and can be kept for milk and meat.

## Activity: Match sheep and goats
You will need: Cards labelled meat, milk, wool, skins, manure, grazing, browsing
1. Sort the cards under the headings Sheep and Goats. Some cards fit both.
2. Explain each choice to another group.
3. Correct any card that was placed without a reason.
4. Write two uses that both animals share and one use that is more typical of goats.

## Practice
1. Give three uses of goats.
2. What is wool a product of?
3. Why must goats be tethered or housed near a vegetable garden?

## Summary
• Sheep are kept mainly for meat, skins and manure, and some give wool.
• Goats give meat, milk, skins and manure, and they browse shrubs.
• Both must be kept out of the crop garden.

### Answers to practice
1. Any three: meat, milk, skins, manure.
2. Some sheep.
3. They browse and will eat the crops if they are left loose.

PAGE 5: Lesson 4: Uses of poultry

LESSON 4: USES OF POULTRY
=========================

## What you will learn
• Match poultry to eggs, meat and manure.
• Explain why fresh poultry manure is not put straight on seedlings.

Curriculum outcomes: b) relate various domestic animals to their uses

## Introduction
A hen can lay an egg every day or so when she is well fed and healthy. That egg is a full packet of food from an animal small enough to keep beside the house.

## Notes
Poultry are domestic birds. Chickens are the main example. Ducks, turkeys and guinea fowl are poultry too.

### Eggs
Hens lay eggs. Eggs are food. They supply protein for the body. Eggs should be collected often, kept clean and dry, and not washed in dirty water. A cracked egg spoils quickly. A cock does not lay eggs. You need hens of laying age, plus feed and clean water, if you want eggs.

### Meat
Chickens, ducks and turkeys are also kept for meat. Chicken meat is a common food at home and at celebrations. Birds kept only for meat may be different from birds kept mainly for eggs, but many household flocks give both.

### Manure
Poultry droppings are rich manure for crops. They are strong when fresh and can burn seedlings. Compost them with grass and leaves, or mix them into a compost heap, before using them in the garden. Then they help vegetables and fruit instead of scorching them.

### Feathers and other uses
Feathers may be used in pillows and decorations. The main food uses to remember are eggs and meat, plus manure for the crops that feed the family.

### A small flock still counts
A farmer does not need a large commercial house to produce food. A few hens in a clean coop, shut in at night to keep them safe from predators, can supply eggs through the week. Shutting them in is also welfare: they are protected from cold rain, thieves and wild animals.

## Key words
• egg — the food laid by a hen
• protein — a nutrient in foods such as eggs and meat that helps the body grow
• coop — a house for poultry

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner spreads fresh chicken droppings on a bed of newly emerged carrot seedlings. The seedlings scorch. What should have been done first?

Working:
1. Fresh poultry manure is too strong for seedlings.
2. It should be composted before it is used on the garden.

Answer: The droppings should have been composted first.

## Activity: Poultry products display
You will need: Pictures of hens, eggs, meat and a compost heap, Cards for ducks, turkeys and guinea fowl
1. Match each bird to the products it can give.
2. Sort products into food for people and manure for crops.
3. Explain why fresh droppings are composted before use.
4. Describe a safe night shelter for a small flock.

## Practice
1. Name two foods we get from poultry.
2. Why is fresh chicken manure not put directly on seedlings?
3. Which bird lays the eggs most homes collect?

## Summary
• Poultry give eggs, meat and manure.
• Compost poultry droppings before using them on crops.
• A small, well-housed flock can supply food at home.

### Answers to practice
1. Eggs and meat.
2. It is too strong and can burn them. It should be composted first.
3. The hen.

PAGE 6: Lesson 5: How domestic animals help food production

LESSON 5: HOW DOMESTIC ANIMALS HELP FOOD PRODUCTION
===================================================

## What you will learn
• Explain direct and indirect ways animals contribute to food.
• Present the importance of domestic animals using examples.

Curriculum outcomes: b) relate various domestic animals to their uses; c) appreciate the importance of domestic animals for food production

## Introduction
Food from animals is not only what is on the plate tonight. Manure under the maize, and an ox that opened the soil, are also part of producing that meal.

## Notes
Domestic animals contribute to food production in two ways.

### Direct food
- Cattle give milk and beef.
- Goats give milk and meat.
- Sheep give mutton.
- Poultry give eggs and meat.

These foods supply protein that helps children grow, and they add variety to meals of grains and vegetables. Milk and eggs can be produced often, without waiting for a harvest season.

### Indirect help
- Manure from all four groups improves soil for crops.
- Oxen plough land so seeds can be sown.
- Animals turn grass and shrubs, which people cannot eat, into milk, meat and eggs, which people can eat.

A household that keeps a cow, or goats, or hens, can eat some of the products and sell some. Selling milk, eggs or an animal pays for other foods, school needs and more feed. In Social Studies this is an economic activity. In Agriculture it is food production.

### What appreciation looks like
Appreciating domestic animals means you can explain these uses clearly and you treat the animals as a resource worth protecting. It does not mean claiming that every family must keep cattle. A family with three hens is already taking part in food production.

Prepare a short talk with one picture or drawing for each animal. For each picture, name one food and one other use. Listen when other groups present, even if their community keeps different animals from yours.

## Key words
• direct food — milk, meat or eggs that people eat from the animal
• indirect — helping food production without itself being the food, such as manure or ploughing

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A farmer has no ox, but her hens' composted droppings are mixed into the vegetable bed and the vegetables do well. How did the hens help food production besides giving eggs?

Working:
1. Eggs are a direct food.
2. Composted droppings are manure, an indirect help to crops.

Answer: Their manure improved the soil for the vegetables.

## Activity: Picture talk on food from animals
You will need: Photos or drawings of cattle, sheep, goats and poultry, Manila paper
1. Give each group one animal.
2. On the paper, write one direct food and one indirect use.
3. Present to the class using the picture, speaking loudly and clearly.
4. Listeners note one new point and thank the group.
5. Together, answer the question: how do domestic animals contribute to food production?

## Practice
1. Give one direct food from cattle and one direct food from poultry.
2. Give two indirect ways domestic animals help food production.
3. Why is keeping hens called food production even when the family eats all the eggs?

## Summary
• Milk, meat and eggs are direct foods from domestic animals.
• Manure and ox ploughing help crops to grow.
• Even a small flock or herd contributes to household food.

### Answers to practice
1. Cattle: milk or beef. Poultry: eggs or meat.
2. Any two: manure for crops, oxen ploughing, turning grass into food people can eat.
3. The eggs are food the household has produced for itself.

PAGE 7: Lesson 6: Caring for domestic animals

LESSON 6: CARING FOR DOMESTIC ANIMALS
=====================================

## What you will learn
• Describe basic welfare needs of domestic animals.
• Explain why poor care reduces food production.

Curriculum outcomes: c) appreciate the importance of domestic animals for food production

## Introduction
A cow with no water gives little milk. A hen in a wet, dirty coop stops laying. The uses we want from animals depend on the care we give them.

## Notes
Animal welfare means meeting the needs of animals so they are not suffering. It is also practical farming. A neglected animal produces less food.

### Five needs
- Water: clean water every day. Animals drink more in hot weather.
- Food: enough pasture, browse or feed for the size of the animal. Poultry need feed, not only scraps that are spoilt.
- Shelter: a boma, shed or coop that keeps off rain, wind and strong sun. Dry bedding reduces disease.
- Safety: protection from predators, thieves and busy roads. Poultry should be shut in at night.
- Health: watch for limping, diarrhoea, coughing or an animal that stays apart. Tell an adult so the animal can be helped. Do not tease or beat animals.

### Handling
Move quietly around cattle so they do not panic. Lead a goat with a rope rather than dragging it by one leg. Collect eggs without chasing hens until they are exhausted. Calm handling keeps animals easier to milk, herd and treat.

### Cleanliness and neighbours
Remove wet manure from the sleeping place so animals are not standing in filth. That manure can go to a compost heap, where it becomes useful. A dirty boma breeds flies that bother both animals and people.

### Why this belongs with food production
Milk, meat and eggs come from healthy, fed animals. When we appreciate domestic animals, we do not only list their products. We give them water, food, shelter and gentle handling so they can keep producing. That is respect for a living thing that feeds the household.

## Key words
• welfare — the health and comfort of an animal under human care
• shelter — a place that protects an animal from weather and danger
• predator — an animal that hunts another animal

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Hens that used to lay well are now crowded in a wet coop with dirty water. Egg numbers have fallen. Which needs are not being met?

Working:
1. The coop is wet, so shelter and cleanliness are poor.
2. The water is dirty, so the need for clean water is not met.

Answer: Clean water, dry shelter and enough space.

## Activity: Welfare check on a picture farm
You will need: A picture or a teacher-described boma and coop, A checklist: water, food, shelter, safety, health
1. Look at each animal in the picture or description.
2. Tick the needs that are met and circle the needs that are missing.
3. Say how the missing need would reduce milk, eggs or growth.
4. Write three welfare rules a learner can follow around domestic animals.

## Practice
1. List four needs of a domestic animal.
2. Why should poultry be shut in at night?
3. How does refusing an animal clean water reduce food production?

## Summary
• Domestic animals need water, food, shelter, safety and health care.
• Gentle handling and clean housing are part of welfare.
• Good care keeps milk, eggs and meat coming.

### Answers to practice
1. Any four: clean water, food, shelter, safety, health care, gentle handling.
2. To protect them from predators, thieves, cold and rain.
3. A thirsty animal gives less milk, fewer eggs or grows poorly.
pages.quiz:
REVISION QUIZ — 2.3 USES OF DOMESTIC ANIMALS
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which animals are the domestic animals in this sub-strand?
   A. Hares, squirrels and monkeys
   B. Cattle, sheep, goats and poultry
   C. Lions, elephants and zebras
   D. Bees, fish and frogs only

2. What makes an animal domestic?
   A. It lives only in a forest
   B. People keep and look after it
   C. It is always bigger than a goat
   D. It never needs water

3. Which product comes from dairy cattle?
   A. Wool
   B. Milk
   C. Eggs
   D. Honey

4. What are oxen used for?

5. Which use is more typical of goats than of sheep on many small farms?
   A. Laying eggs
   B. Pulling heavy ploughs
   C. Producing milk
   D. Growing wool

6. Name two foods from poultry.

7. Why compost chicken droppings before putting them on seedlings?
   A. Fresh droppings are too strong and can burn plants
   B. Chickens need the droppings as feed
   C. Compost removes all the nutrients
   D. Seedlings only grow in sand

8. How does manure help food production?

9. A cow gives little milk and her water trough is empty. What is the most likely welfare problem?
   A. She has too much shade
   B. She lacks clean water
   C. She has laid too many eggs
   D. She is eating too much wool

10. Which sentence shows appreciation of domestic animals?
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 2.3 USES OF DOMESTIC ANIMALS
========================================

1. B. Cattle, sheep, goats and poultry
   Cattle, sheep, goats and poultry are the domestic animals learners match to uses.

2. B. People keep and look after it
   Domestic animals are kept by people, who provide care and use the products.

3. B. Milk
   Dairy cattle are kept for milk. Eggs come from poultry and wool from some sheep.

4. Pulling ploughs and carts.
   Oxen provide draught power that helps farmers prepare land for crops.

5. C. Producing milk
   Goats are commonly kept for meat and milk. Wool is a sheep product, and oxen pull ploughs.

6. Eggs and meat.
   Hens lay eggs, and poultry are also kept for meat. Their droppings are manure, not a food for people.

7. A. Fresh droppings are too strong and can burn plants
   Fresh poultry manure can scorch young plants. Composting makes it safer and still useful.

8. It feeds the soil so crops grow better.
   Manure is an indirect contribution. The animal helps the crops that people eat.

9. B. She lacks clean water
   Animals need clean water every day. Without it, milk production falls.

10. We use their milk, meat, eggs and manure, and we give them food, water and shelter.
   Appreciation includes both recognising their role in food production and caring for their welfare.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Uses of cattle
studyPages.body:
LESSON 2: USES OF CATTLE
========================

## What you will learn
• Match cattle to the products and work they provide.
• Distinguish a dairy animal from an ox used for work.

Curriculum outcomes: b) relate various domestic animals to their uses

A family keeps two oxen for ploughing and one cow that is milked each day. Match each animal to its main use.

Working:
1. Oxen are trained to pull ploughs and carts.
2. A cow that is milked is kept for milk.

Answer: The oxen are used for draught power. The cow is used for milk.

You will need: Manila paper, Pictures or drawings of a cow, an ox, milk, meat, a hide and manure
1. Draw or pin a cow and an ox on the chart.
2. Draw lines to their uses: milk, meat, hides, ploughing and manure.
3. Discuss which uses feed people directly and which help crops grow.
4. Present the chart in one minute.

## Practice
1. Name three uses of cattle.
2. What are oxen mainly used for?
3. How does cattle manure help food production?

## Summary
• Cattle give milk, meat, hides and manure.
• Oxen provide draught power for ploughing and carts.
• Manure links cattle keeping to crop growing.

### Answers to practice
1. Any three: milk, meat, hides, pulling ploughs or carts, manure.
2. Pulling ploughs and carts.
3. It feeds the soil so crops grow better.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Uses of sheep and goats
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: USES OF SHEEP AND GOATS
=================================

## What you will learn
• State the uses of sheep and of goats.
• Explain one way goats fit places with shrubs and little grass.

Curriculum outcomes: b) relate various domestic animals to their uses

## Introduction
Sheep and goats are smaller than cattle, so a family with a small piece of land can keep them. Their uses overlap, but they are not the same animal.

## Notes
### Sheep
Sheep are kept mainly for meat, called mutton. Their skins are used for leather. Droppings are used as manure. Some sheep grow wool, which is spun into yarn and used for clothing. Many sheep kept in Kenya are kept first for meat rather than for a heavy wool clip, so do not assume every sheep is a wool sheep. Look at the animals in your own community.

Sheep prefer to graze short grass. They are usually herded in a group called a flock.

### Goats
Goats are kept for meat, and many are also kept for milk. Goat milk is a food, just as cow milk is. Skins are used for leather. Droppings are strong manure and should be composted before they are put on young plants.

Goats browse. They eat leaves and shrubs as well as grass. Because of this they can be kept where the pasture is bushy. They are agile and will eat crops if they are not tethered or housed. A goat in the vegetable garden is not 'using' the goat well. It is a failure of care.

### Comparing them
Both give meat, skins and manure. Goats are the ones more often milked on small farms. Sheep are the ones that may give wool. Neither replaces cattle when a farmer needs a heavy ox for ploughing.

When you match animals to uses, use a table with two columns so sheep and goats are not muddled into one animal.

## Key words
• mutton — meat from sheep
• browse — to eat leaves and twigs of shrubs
• flock — a group of sheep or goats kept together

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A household in a bushy area wants milk and meat from a small animal that can eat shrubs. Should they choose a sheep or a goat? Give one reason.

Working:
1. Goats browse on shrubs and many are kept for milk as well as meat.
2. Sheep mainly graze grass and are kept mainly for meat.

Answer: A goat, because it browses shrubs and can be kept for milk and meat.

## Activity: Match sheep and goats
You will need: Cards labelled meat, milk, wool, skins, manure, grazing, browsing
1. Sort the cards under the headings Sheep and Goats. Some cards fit both.
2. Explain each choice to another group.
3. Correct any card that was placed without a reason.
4. Write two uses that both animals share and one use that is more typical of goats.

## Practice
1. Give three uses of goats.
2. What is wool a product of?
3. Why must goats be tethered or housed near a vegetable garden?

## Summary
• Sheep are kept mainly for meat, skins and manure, and some give wool.
• Goats give meat, milk, skins and manure, and they browse shrubs.
• Both must be kept out of the crop garden.

### Answers to practice
1. Any three: meat, milk, skins, manure.
2. Some sheep.
3. They browse and will eat the crops if they are left loose.

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: Uses of poultry
studyPages.body:
LESSON 4: USES OF POULTRY
=========================

## What you will learn
• Match poultry to eggs, meat and manure.
• Explain why fresh poultry manure is not put straight on seedlings.

Curriculum outcomes: b) relate various domestic animals to their uses

## Introduction
A hen can lay an egg every day or so when she is well fed and healthy. That egg is a full packet of food from an animal small enough to keep beside the house.

## Notes
Poultry are domestic birds. Chickens are the main example. Ducks, turkeys and guinea fowl are poultry too.

### Eggs
Hens lay eggs. Eggs are food. They supply protein for the body. Eggs should be collected often, kept clean and dry, and not washed in dirty water. A cracked egg spoils quickly. A cock does not lay eggs. You need hens of laying age, plus feed and clean water, if you want eggs.

### Meat
Chickens, ducks and turkeys are also kept for meat. Chicken meat is a common food at home and at celebrations. Birds kept only for meat may be different from birds kept mainly for eggs, but many household flocks give both.

### Manure
Poultry droppings are rich manure for crops. They are strong when fresh and can burn seedlings. Compost them with grass and leaves, or mix them into a compost heap, before using them in the garden. Then they help vegetables and fruit instead of scorching them.

### Feathers and other uses
Feathers may be used in pillows and decorations. The main food uses to remember are eggs and meat, plus manure for the crops that feed the family.

### A small flock still counts
A farmer does not need a large commercial house to produce food. A few hens in a clean coop, shut in at night to keep them safe from predators, can supply eggs through the week. Shutting them in is also welfare: they are protected from cold rain, thieves and wild animals.

## Key words
• egg — the food laid by a hen
• protein — a nutrient in foods such as eggs and meat that helps the body grow
• coop — a house for poultry

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner spreads fresh chicken droppings on a bed of newly emerged carrot seedlings. The seedlings scorch. What should have been done first?

Working:
1. Fresh poultry manure is too strong for seedlings.
2. It should be composted before it is used on the garden.

Answer: The droppings should have been composted first.

## Activity: Poultry products display
You will need: Pictures of hens, eggs, meat and a compost heap, Cards for ducks, turkeys and guinea fowl
1. Match each bird to the products it can give.
2. Sort products into food for people and manure for crops.
3. Explain why fresh droppings are composted before use.
4. Describe a safe night shelter for a small flock.

## Practice
1. Name two foods we get from poultry.
2. Why is fresh chicken manure not put directly on seedlings?
3. Which bird lays the eggs most homes collect?

## Summary
• Poultry give eggs, meat and manure.
• Compost poultry droppings before using them on crops.
• A small, well-housed flock can supply food at home.

### Answers to practice
1. Eggs and meat.
2. It is too strong and can burn them. It should be composted first.
3. The hen.

studyPages.title: Lesson 5: How domestic animals help food production
studyPages.body:
LESSON 5: HOW DOMESTIC ANIMALS HELP FOOD PRODUCTION
===================================================

## What you will learn
• Explain direct and indirect ways animals contribute to food.
• Present the importance of domestic animals using examples.

Curriculum outcomes: b) relate various domestic animals to their uses; c) appreciate the importance of domestic animals for food production

## Introduction
Food from animals is not only what is on the plate tonight. Manure under the maize, and an ox that opened the soil, are also part of producing that meal.

## Notes
Domestic animals contribute to food production in two ways.

### Direct food
- Cattle give milk and beef.
- Goats give milk and meat.
- Sheep give mutton.
- Poultry give eggs and meat.

These foods supply protein that helps children grow, and they add variety to meals of grains and vegetables. Milk and eggs can be produced often, without waiting for a harvest season.

### Indirect help
- Manure from all four groups improves soil for crops.
- Oxen plough land so seeds can be sown.
- Animals turn grass and shrubs, which people cannot eat, into milk, meat and eggs, which people can eat.

A household that keeps a cow, or goats, or hens, can eat some of the products and sell some. Selling milk, eggs or an animal pays for other foods, school needs and more feed. In Social Studies this is an economic activity. In Agriculture it is food production.

### What appreciation looks like
Appreciating domestic animals means you can explain these uses clearly and you treat the animals as a resource worth protecting. It does not mean claiming that every family must keep cattle. A family with three hens is already taking part in food production.

Prepare a short talk with one picture or drawing for each animal. For each picture, name one food and one other use. Listen when other groups present, even if their community keeps different animals from yours.

## Key words
• direct food — milk, meat or eggs that people eat from the animal
• indirect — helping food production without itself being the food, such as manure or ploughing

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A farmer has no ox, but her hens' composted droppings are mixed into the vegetable bed and the vegetables do well. How did the hens help food production besides giving eggs?

Working:
1. Eggs are a direct food.
2. Composted droppings are manure, an indirect help to crops.

Answer: Their manure improved the soil for the vegetables.

## Activity: Picture talk on food from animals
You will need: Photos or drawings of cattle, sheep, goats and poultry, Manila paper
1. Give each group one animal.
2. On the paper, write one direct food and one indirect use.
3. Present to the class using the picture, speaking loudly and clearly.
4. Listeners note one new point and thank the group.
5. Together, answer the question: how do domestic animals contribute to food production?

## Practice
1. Give one direct food from cattle and one direct food from poultry.
2. Give two indirect ways domestic animals help food production.
3. Why is keeping hens called food production even when the family eats all the eggs?

## Summary
• Milk, meat and eggs are direct foods from domestic animals.
• Manure and ox ploughing help crops to grow.
• Even a small flock or herd contributes to household food.

### Answers to practice
1. Cattle: milk or beef. Poultry: eggs or meat.
2. Any two: manure for crops, oxen ploughing, turning grass into food people can eat.
3. The eggs are food the household has produced for itself.

studyPages.title: Lesson 6: Caring for domestic animals
studyPages.body:
LESSON 6: CARING FOR DOMESTIC ANIMALS
=====================================

## What you will learn
• Describe basic welfare needs of domestic animals.
• Explain why poor care reduces food production.

Curriculum outcomes: c) appreciate the importance of domestic animals for food production

## Introduction
A cow with no water gives little milk. A hen in a wet, dirty coop stops laying. The uses we want from animals depend on the care we give them.

## Notes
Animal welfare means meeting the needs of animals so they are not suffering. It is also practical farming. A neglected animal produces less food.

### Five needs
- Water: clean water every day. Animals drink more in hot weather.
- Food: enough pasture, browse or feed for the size of the animal. Poultry need feed, not only scraps that are spoilt.
- Shelter: a boma, shed or coop that keeps off rain, wind and strong sun. Dry bedding reduces disease.
- Safety: protection from predators, thieves and busy roads. Poultry should be shut in at night.
- Health: watch for limping, diarrhoea, coughing or an animal that stays apart. Tell an adult so the animal can be helped. Do not tease or beat animals.

### Handling
Move quietly around cattle so they do not panic. Lead a goat with a rope rather than dragging it by one leg. Collect eggs without chasing hens until they are exhausted. Calm handling keeps animals easier to milk, herd and treat.

### Cleanliness and neighbours
Remove wet manure from the sleeping place so animals are not standing in filth. That manure can go to a compost heap, where it becomes useful. A dirty boma breeds flies that bother both animals and people.

### Why this belongs with food production
Milk, meat and eggs come from healthy, fed animals. When we appreciate domestic animals, we do not only list their products. We give them water, food, shelter and gentle handling so they can keep producing. That is respect for a living thing that feeds the household.

## Key words
• welfare — the health and comfort of an animal under human care
• shelter — a place that protects an animal from weather and danger
• predator — an animal that hunts another animal

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Hens that used to lay well are now crowded in a wet coop with dirty water. Egg numbers have fallen. Which needs are not being met?

Working:
1. The coop is wet, so shelter and cleanliness are poor.
2. The water is dirty, so the need for clean water is not met.

Answer: Clean water, dry shelter and enough space.

## Activity: Welfare check on a picture farm
You will need: A picture or a teacher-described boma and coop, A checklist: water, food, shelter, safety, health
1. Look at each animal in the picture or description.
2. Tick the needs that are met and circle the needs that are missing.
3. Say how the missing need would reduce milk, eggs or growth.
4. Write three welfare rules a learner can follow around domestic animals.

## Practice
1. List four needs of a domestic animal.
2. Why should poultry be shut in at night?
3. How does refusing an animal clean water reduce food production?

## Summary
• Domestic animals need water, food, shelter, safety and health care.
• Gentle handling and clean housing are part of welfare.
• Good care keeps milk, eggs and meat coming.

### Answers to practice
1. Any four: clean water, food, shelter, safety, health care, gentle handling.
2. To protect them from predators, thieves, cold and rain.
3. A thirsty animal gives less milk, fewer eggs or grows poorly.

questions.question: Which animals are the domestic animals in this sub-strand?
questions.explanation: Cattle, sheep, goats and poultry are the domestic animals learners match to uses.

questions.question: What makes an animal domestic?
options: It lives only in a forest
People keep and look after it
It is always bigger than a goat
questions.explanation: Domestic animals are kept by people, who provide care and use the products.

questions.question: Which product comes from dairy cattle?
questions.explanation: Dairy cattle are kept for milk. Eggs come from poultry and wool from some sheep.

questions.question: What are oxen used for?
questions.explanation: Oxen provide draught power that helps farmers prepare land for crops.

questions.question: Which use is more typical of goats than of sheep on many small farms?
questions.explanation: Goats are commonly kept for meat and milk. Wool is a sheep product, and oxen pull ploughs.

questions.question: Name two foods from poultry.
questions.explanation: Hens lay eggs, and poultry are also kept for meat. Their droppings are manure, not a food for people.

questions.question: Why compost chicken droppings before putting them on seedlings?
options: Fresh droppings are too strong and can burn plants
Chickens need the droppings as feed
questions.explanation: Fresh poultry manure can scorch young plants. Composting makes it safer and still useful.

questions.question: How does manure help food production?
questions.answer: It feeds the soil so crops grow better.
questions.explanation: Manure is an indirect contribution. The animal helps the crops that people eat.

questions.question: A cow gives little milk and her water trough is empty. What is the most likely welfare problem?
options: She has laid too many eggs
She is eating too much wool
questions.explanation: Animals need clean water every day. Without it, milk production falls.

questions.question: Which sentence shows appreciation of domestic animals?
questions.answer: We use their milk, meat, eggs and manure, and we give them food, water and shelter.
questions.explanation: Appreciation includes both recognising their role in food production and caring for their welfare.
